disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c of 5.7% is in the prediabetes range, which means this is a good time to focus on prevention rather than something to be alarmed about. Your weight, age, and existing blood pressure and cholesterol concerns all add to your overall risk, so it's worth paying attention to these together. The most valuable next steps are keeping up with your highlighted monitoring—lipid profile, kidney function, and blood pressure checks—staying active most days, and following the food guidance around sodium, fibre, and healthy fats. These small, steady steps can make a real difference over time.

risk_factors.label: Body weight above the healthy range
Existing health condition: High blood pressure
Existing health condition: High cholesterol or triglycerides

comorbidity_assessment.note: Blood pressure and blood sugar often influence each other, and both benefit from regular activity, lower sodium intake, and a DASH-style eating pattern.
Higher blood sugar levels can affect cholesterol and triglyceride levels, so keeping saturated fat low and including soluble fibre can support healthier numbers for both.

constraints: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total); avoid pickles, papad, instant noodles and salty snacks.
Follow a DASH-style pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and low-fat dairy (or fortified alternatives).
Keep saturated fat low (limit ghee, butter, coconut oil, red and processed meat); avoid trans fats (vanaspati, many fried and bakery foods).
Include soluble fibre daily (oats, barley, pulses, psyllium) and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, olive or mustard oil in small amounts).

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens such as spinach and kale
Whole grains like oats, barley and brown rice
Pulses including lentils, chickpeas and beans
Fresh fruits such as berries, apples and citrus
Unsalted nuts and seeds like walnuts, almonds and flaxseed
Lean proteins such as skinless chicken, turkey and fish
Low-fat dairy or fortified plant alternatives
Olive oil in small amounts for cooking
foods_to_avoid: Instant noodles and other processed convenience foods
Red and processed meats like bacon and sausages
Butter, ghee and coconut oil in large amounts
Fried and bakery items made with trans fats (vanaspati)
White bread, refined flour products and white rice in excess
Canned soups and sauces high in sodium
plan.portion_guidance: Use a standard dinner plate and fill half with non-starchy vegetables, a quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables, and a quarter with lean protein. Use measuring cups for grains and pulses, and keep added fats to about one teaspoon per meal. A small handful equals about one ounce for nuts and seeds.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 cups (64 ounces) of water a day. Herbal tea and water infused with lemon or cucumber are good options. Limit sugary drinks and keep caffeinated beverages moderate.
based_on: high blood pressure: DASH-style, low sodium
high cholesterol or triglycerides: low saturated fat, soluble fibre

exercise: Start with 15-20 minutes of moderate aerobic activity like brisk walking or swimming most days, building gradually toward 150 minutes a week, since regular moderate aerobic activity helps lower blood pressure and improves HDL cholesterol and triglycerides.
Add simple muscle-strengthening exercises, such as bodyweight squats or light resistance bands, on 2 non-consecutive days each week.
Warm up and cool down gently, and increase intensity slowly given your current activity level.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk daily this week, then increase by a few minutes every few days until you reach at least 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week.
lifestyle.weight_management: Since your BMI falls in the overweight category, gradually working toward a modest reduction in body weight through steady activity and balanced eating can support healthier blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar levels over time. Small, sustainable changes work better than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens before bed, and keep your bedroom cool and dark to support restful sleep.
stress: Try slow, deep breathing exercises for 5-10 minutes a day to help calm your body and support healthy blood pressure.
Consider a short daily mindfulness or meditation practice, even just 10 minutes, to help manage stress.
Gentle activities like stretching or time outdoors can also help lower stress levels.
behaviour_change: Build your aerobic activity gradually, since consistent moderate exercise supports both blood pressure and cholesterol improvements over time.
Track your walking and strength sessions in a simple log or app to notice progress and stay motivated.
Consider connecting with a friend or group for shared walks, which can make it easier to stick with new habits.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

preventive_actions: Aim for regular moderate aerobic activity most days of the week, such as brisk walking, to support blood pressure and cholesterol.
Keep sodium intake under 2,300 mg a day by avoiding pickles, papad, and salty snacks.
Include soluble fibre like oats, barley, and pulses daily to support steady blood sugar and healthy cholesterol.
Choose unsaturated fats such as nuts, seeds, and olive or mustard oil instead of ghee, butter, or coconut oil.
Keep track of your calorie target of 1200 calories a day as part of a balanced eating pattern.
Schedule your lipid profile, kidney function, and blood pressure checks as part of regular monitoring.
